claims.text: Tailored thermo-mechanical processing can simultaneously improve the strength and room-temperature tensile ductility of eutectic high-entropy alloys.
The initial alloy has coarse dual-phase lamellar colonies.
Internal boundaries in coarse lamellar colonies are sites where microcracks can initiate during tensile loading.
Cold rolling or moderate plastic deformation followed by optimized annealing is a suitable thermo-mechanical processing route.
The thermo-mechanical treatment breaks down and refines the original coarse lamellar colonies.
The intervention produces an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that retains a hierarchical lamellar character.
The refined microstructure has well-distributed internal boundaries.
The ultrafine hierarchical duplex structure creates a two-hierarchical constraint effect.
Refinement increases the density of phase boundaries.
The increased phase-boundary density impedes dislocation motion and thereby strengthens the alloy.
The refined microstructure generates a microcrack-arresting mechanism that enhances ductility.
Phase boundaries themselves provide the effective sites that arrest microcracks.
Relative to the coarse lamellar baseline, the processed alloy will have higher tensile strength.
Relative to the coarse lamellar baseline, the processed alloy will have greater room-temperature tensile ductility.
Conventional casting produces the coarse dual-phase lamellar baseline with limited ductility.
The intervention is applicable to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy system.
Excessive annealing can cause grain coarsening or loss of lamellar morphology and diminish the intervention's benefits.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in both strength and ductility, or observation of earlier excessive microcracking, would falsify the hypothesis.
